title: Ames: justifying trust leans on Christ — special assurance is later and separable
source_text: CXVI. Nam manifestum fecimus longe plurimos Scholae Reformatae Doctores, fiduciam illam non habere pro conditione sub qua, vel instrumento per quod justificemur. Et primo quidem istud ita clare de Amesio ostendimus, ut nullus possit esse dubitationi locus. Quandoquidem, ut patet, ex testimoniis ejus ante citatis, docet proprie peccata remitti, adeoque nos justificari, per actum illum fiduciae qua Christo innitimur, vel in misericordiam Dei per ipsum reclinamus: qui natura praecedit actum istum quo credimus peccata jam esse remissa. Fiduciam illam per quam justificamur esse actum voluntatis, non autem intellectus; adeoque objectum fidei quatenus justificat non esse veritatem alicujus propositionis, qualis est haec, mihi sunt per Christum remissa peccata; sed Christum ipsum, vel Dei misericordiam in Christo. Item salvificam fidem qua in Deum credimus, esse quidem veram ac propriam fiduciam: Verum non qua hac voce notatur certa & absoluta persuasio de bono futuro, sed qua significat electionem & apprehensionem sufficientis ac idonei medii, ac in quo persuasio & exspectatio talis fundatur. Quo sensu dicuntur homines fiduciam habere in sapientia, potentia, amicis, & opibus suis. Et sic credere in Deum, esse credendo adhaerere Deo, inniti Deo, acquiescere in Deo, tanquam in vita & salute nostra omni sufficiente. Proinde quemadmodum assensus generalis quem Dei Verbo adhibemus non est fides salvifica, quia potest esse sine ulla vita; ita quoque assensum specialem, quo statuimus Deum esse Deum nostrum in Christo, non esse actum primum fidei, sed solum actum ex fide emanantem. Verum fiduciam illam quam habet pro actu fidei proprio, & cui tribuit nostram justificationem, esse medium inter assensum generalem, quo firmiter credit aliquis veras esse promissiones factas credentibus & resipiscentibus, & inter assensum specialem, quo credit aliquis se divinae gratiae jam esse participem. Quoniam assensus ille generalis fiduciam istam parit, assensus vero specialis ex eadem fiducia fluit. Nec tamen vult ex ista fiducia qua Deo innitimur & ei adhaeremus, sic fluere istum assensum specialem, quo percipimus & apprehendimus gratiae jam factae possessionem actualem, quin possit, saltem ad tempus, ab ea separari: non enim omnes justificatos mox certos esse de sua justificatione; & experientiam docere, particularem istam certiorationem intellectus in quibusdam deesse ad tempus, qui tamen fidem veram in cordibus suis habent interim latentem.
pass_a_gloss: For we have made manifest that by far most Doctors of the Reformed School do not take that trust as the condition under which, or the instrument through which, we are justified. And first indeed we have shown this so clearly concerning Ames that there can be no room for doubt. Since, as is plain from his testimonies cited before, he teaches that sins are properly remitted, and so we are justified, through that act of trust by which we lean on Christ, or recline upon God's mercy through him: which by nature precedes that act by which we believe sins have already been remitted. That trust through which we are justified is an act of the will, not of the intellect; and so the object of faith insofar as it justifies is not the truth of some proposition such as this — my sins have been remitted through Christ — but Christ himself, or God's mercy in Christ. Likewise, the saving faith by which we believe in God is indeed true and proper trust: yet not that by which this word denotes a certain and absolute persuasion of a future good, but that by which it signifies the choice and apprehension of a sufficient and suitable means, and that in which such persuasion and expectation is founded. In which sense people are said to have trust in their wisdom, power, friends, and wealth. And so to believe in God is, by believing, to adhere to God, lean on God, rest in God, as in our life and salvation all-sufficient. Therefore just as the general assent we give to God's Word is not saving faith, because it can be without any life; so also the special assent by which we judge God to be our God in Christ is not the first act of faith, but only an act flowing from faith. But that trust which he takes as faith's proper act, and to which he attributes our justification, is a middle between the general assent by which someone firmly believes the promises made to believers and penitents are true, and the special assent by which someone believes he is already a partaker of divine grace. Because that general assent begets this trust, while the special assent flows from the same trust. Yet he does not hold that from this trust by which we lean on God and adhere to him, that special assent by which we perceive and apprehend actual possession of grace already granted must so flow that it cannot, at least for a time, be separated from it: for not all who are justified are immediately certain of their justification; and experience teaches that that particular assurance of the intellect is for a time lacking in some who nonetheless have true faith lying hidden meanwhile in their hearts.
pass_b_english: Most Reformed doctors — Ames clearest — do not make already-granted remission the condition or instrument of justification.

Ames: we are justified by will's trust that leans on Christ / God's mercy — which naturally precedes believing sins are already remitted. Faith's justifying object is Christ (or mercy in him), not the proposition 'my sins are forgiven.'
Saving 'trust' here means choosing and resting on a sufficient means, not absolute persuasion of a future good — as one trusts friends or wealth.

General Word-assent is not saving; special 'God is my God' assent flows from faith rather than being its first act. Justifying trust sits between general assent and special grace-possession — and the latter can be temporarily absent in true believers.
